title: The good friend who chooses
hookLine: the friend who closes your menu and orders for you; should a teacher choose your practice, or should you test it yourself?
tomorrow: a house, family, even books. what could they get in the way of?

cards: At a new restaurant, there's always that one friend who closes your menu and says: trust me, i'll order. Some people love that friend. Some would rather go hungry.
Buddhaghosa's answer to who should choose your meditation subject sounds like the menu friend: traditionally, the teacher does. And inside the tradition, that answer has a strong rival.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: THE GOOD FRIEND CHOOSES.
teach.b: View one: the Visuddhimagga. Go to a good friend, a kalyanamitta, someone who knows the path, who can watch how you live and then give you the subject that fits.
Temperament is hard to read from the inside; the one holding the broom rarely sees the dust. Behind this sits an exchange from the suttas.

teach.h: NOT HALF THE HOLY LIFE: ALL OF IT.
teach.b: Ananda says good friendship is half of the holy life, and the Buddha answers: not so. It's the whole of it. View two: the Kalama Sutta.
The Kalamas tell the Buddha they're confused, since every teacher who passes through praises his own way.
He tells them: don't go by reports, or tradition, or scripture, or clever reasoning, or because this teacher is ours.
When you know for yourselves that something leads to harm, drop it. When you know it leads to good, take it up. Now, each side's best case.

teach.h: BLIND SPOTS VS. A WRONG TEACHER.
teach.b: The Kalama side protects you from a teacher who's wrong, or worse; it keeps your own eyes open. The good-friend side protects you from your blind spots; nobody sees the back of their own head.
And they may not cancel each other out.
In Buddhaghosa's picture, the friend chooses, and you still find out in your own practice whether it helps. A friend chooses. You do the walking.

how: In Theravada monasteries and meditation centers, a student may receive a meditation subject from a teacher and report back on how it goes; lay meditators can check their practice with a teacher too.

games.q: what does “the good friend who chooses” mean?
o: a classmate who meditates beside you for motivation
a guardian spirit believed to watch over meditators
a trusted teacher who reads you and picks your practice

p: a good friend gives the subject
good friendship is half the holy life
not half: the whole of it

s: the Buddha called good friendship half of the holy life
that was Ananda's guess. the Buddha answered: not so, it's the whole of it.
the Kalama Sutta says not to accept a teaching just because 'this teacher is ours'
know for yourselves what leads to harm and what leads to good.
in the Visuddhimagga, a student picks a subject alone from the list
traditionally the teacher, the good friend, gives it after watching how the student lives.

games.q: your friend says: "nobody should choose your path for you. the Buddha said test everything yourself." what's the best case for letting a teacher choose?
o: a good friend sees your blind spots, and you still test what they give.
teachers have authority, so questioning them is disrespectful.
the Kalama Sutta doesn't really count; it's a minor teaching.
games.why: both views stand in the tradition. the good friend covers what you can't see in yourself; the Kalama Sutta keeps your own eyes open. a friend chooses; you do the walking.

practice: Think of one person who has seen you at your best and at your worst. Write them a short question that only someone who knows you could answer, like: what am i good at that i can't see?
Send it, or keep it as a version until it feels right.

wordCard.voice: The good friend who chooses: in the Visuddhimagga, the kalyanamitta, the teacher who reads you and gives the meditation subject.

orig.note: Pali: good friend, admirable friend; in meditation, the teacher who gives the subject.

carryVoice: Something to keep: a friend chooses, and you still do the walking. Three of forty, done.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga III.28, III.57–65 (approach the good friend, the giver of the meditation subject)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (good friendship is the whole of the holy life)
Anguttara Nikaya 3.65, Kalama Sutta (do not go by reports, tradition, scripture, reasoning, or 'this teacher is ours'; know for yourselves)
